260.title: Catholic: the Mass
260.hook: Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine
260.howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday, and some go daily, receiving Communion; many also pray quietly before the tabernacle, where a sanctuary lamp burns to show the consecrated bread is kept there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Christmas, the baby in the manger. Your line was a child in the cold. Did your small gift reach someone? Day two hundred sixty, and a new visit: the Catholic tradition.

A Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. Quiet. A few people sit scattered in the pews, not talking, not reading, just there. Near the front, beside a small locked box, a candle is burning in red glass. It burns day and night. Ask one of the people sitting there why they came, and the answer might be a nod toward that box, and three words: because he's here. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition, we start at the center: the Eucharist, and what Catholics call the real presence.
screen: `A QUIET CHURCH, A WEEKDAY.` → `A RED CANDLE THAT NEVER GOES OUT.` → `BECAUSE HE'S HERE.`

segments.voice: Eucharist is a Greek word: thanksgiving. It's kin to charis, grace, from a few days ago. It names the meal at the heart of the Mass, which goes back to the night before Jesus died. At a Passover-season supper with his disciples, he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them. In the Douay-Rheims translation: "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." Then the cup: his blood of the covenant. And, in Luke's telling, do this in memory of me. Catholics take those words at their plainest. They believe that at Mass, when the priest says Jesus' words over the bread and wine, they become the body and blood of Christ: still looking and tasting like bread and wine, but truly him. The Church's word for this, from the Middle Ages, is transubstantiation, a change in what the thing most deeply is. That's why it's called the real presence. And that's what the little box, the tabernacle, holds: consecrated bread kept after Mass, for the sick and for prayer. The red lamp says someone is home. Christians understand this meal differently, and it's worth saying who says what. Orthodox Christians also believe Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a holy mystery rather than define how. Lutherans speak of a real presence too, in their own terms. Many other Protestants see the meal as a powerful remembrance and sign. The Second Vatican Council called the Eucharist the source and summit of the whole Christian life, and so, for Catholics, a quiet church is never really empty.
screen: `EUCHARIST — THANKSGIVING.` · `TAKE YE, AND EAT. THIS IS MY BODY.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND THE RED LAMP.` · `WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE MEAL.` · then, large: `REAL PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you like, and if one is near, you can sit in a quiet church sometime this week; the doors of many are open by day. For now, sit wherever you are and practice presence the simple way. Notice what is really here: your breath, the weight of your body, the sounds in the room. No need to add anything. Just be present to what's present. The bell holds the time.
Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the meal of the Mass, where Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine. Today's word.
Your line: real presence. Today, give one person your real presence: phone down, eyes up, listening all the way. Day two hundred sixty.

261.title: Catholic: the rosary
261.hook: beads, prayers, and the stories of Jesus and Mary, one decade at a time
261.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the rosary daily or weekly, alone or in groups, often praying one set of mysteries assigned to each day of the week; October is traditionally the month of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Eucharist, and the red lamp that never goes out. Your line was real presence. Who got your full attention? Day two hundred sixty-one.

Maybe you've seen one hanging from a rearview mirror. Or wrapped around a grandmother's fingers in a hospital waiting room, her lips moving without a sound. Or laid in the hands of someone at a funeral. A loop of beads with a small cross at the end. It looks like jewelry, but the people who pray with it say it's something you do, not something you wear. Its rhythm has carried people through long nights, long drives and long grief. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the rosary.
screen: `A REARVIEW MIRROR.` → `A GRANDMOTHER'S FINGERS.` → `SOMETHING YOU DO, NOT WEAR.`

segments.voice: The word comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers offered like roses. Here's how it works. The beads are grouped in tens, called decades, usually five on a rosary. Each decade begins on a single bead with the Our Father, the prayer we met last week. Then ten Hail Marys, one per bead, a prayer we'll open properly in a few days. Then a short Glory Be. And while the fingers move and the lips repeat, the mind is somewhere else: in a story. Each decade is paired with a scene from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called a mystery. The joyful mysteries include the angel's visit to Mary and the birth in Bethlehem. The sorrowful mysteries walk through the arrest and the crucifixion. The glorious mysteries begin with the resurrection. In 2002, Pope John Paul the Second added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus' public life, like his baptism and the Last Supper. So the rosary is really two things at once: a repetition for the body and a meditation for the mind. The beads keep count, so you don't have to. Where did it come from? A popular tradition says Mary gave it to Saint Dominic in the thirteenth century. Historians tend to see it growing more gradually, out of medieval monks praying the hundred and fifty psalms, and laypeople who couldn't read saying a hundred and fifty short prayers instead. Either way, it grew up for people with busy hands and no books.
screen: `ROSARIUM — A ROSE GARDEN.` · `DECADES: ONE OUR FATHER, TEN HAIL MARYS.` · `EACH DECADE, A MYSTERY TO PONDER.` · `REPETITION FOR THE BODY, STORY FOR THE MIND.` · then, large: `ONE BEAD AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you have beads, hold them. If not, a string with ten knots, or simply your ten fingers. Move through them slowly, one breath per bead. If you pray, you can say a prayer you know on each one; if not, let each breath be a quiet thank-you. Let your mind rest on one scene, a birth, a table, a sunrise. One bead at a time. The bell holds the time.
Rosary. From rosarium, a rose garden: beads counted in decades, each one carrying a story of Jesus and Mary. Today's word.
Your line: one bead at a time. Today, when something feels too big, do only the next small piece, and then the next. Day two hundred sixty-one.

262.title: Catholic: the saints
262.hook: Catholics speak of the communion of saints, friends in heaven who pray with the living (Hebrews 12:1)
262.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate saints' feast days through the year and All Saints' Day on November 1, take a saint's name at confirmation, and ask saints to pray for them, often through a patron saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rosary, prayers counted in decades. Your line was one bead at a time. Did something big get done one small piece at a time? Day two hundred sixty-two.

Picture the last mile of a marathon. Your legs are gone. You're sure you can't finish. And then you hear it: the crowd along the barriers, thousands of strangers shouting your name off the bib on your chest. Somehow you keep going. Now imagine that crowd isn't strangers. It's everyone who ran this course before you, who hit the same wall and got through, and they're still watching, still cheering. That's close to how Catholics picture the saints. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the communion of saints.
screen: `THE LAST MILE OF A MARATHON.` → `A CROWD SHOUTING YOUR NAME.` → `EVERYONE WHO RAN IT BEFORE.`

segments.voice: The picture comes from the letter to the Hebrews. After a long list of faithful people from the Hebrew Bible, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and more, the writer says, in the King James Version: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight." And run the race. A cloud, meaning a great crowd. Witnesses, people who've seen it through. Saint comes from the Latin sanctus, holy. In the New Testament, Paul calls all believers saints. Over time the Church also began to honor particular people, first the martyrs, then others, whose lives showed holiness clearly. Today Catholics recognize some of them formally through a long process called canonization. The Apostles' Creed, said by many Christians, includes the line I believe in the communion of saints. For Catholics that means the Church isn't only the people in the pews: it includes those who have died in Christ, and the bond isn't broken by death. So Catholics ask the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. Catholics are careful to say they honor saints and ask for their prayers; worship belongs to God alone. There are patron saints for almost everything: Francis for animals, Anthony for lost things, Joseph for workers and fathers. Christians differ here. Orthodox Christians also honor the saints and ask their prayers, often through icons. Many Protestants honor faithful people of the past as examples, but don't ask them to pray, preferring to pray to God directly. Either way, the old letter's picture holds: you are not the first to run this.
screen: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.` · `SANCTUS — HOLY.` · `DEATH DOESN'T BREAK THE BOND.` · `HONORED, ASKED TO PRAY, NOT WORSHIPED.` · then, large: `A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a person who inspires you. Sit, and let your own cloud of witnesses gather. A grandparent. A teacher. Someone from history. A saint, if you have one. People who ran their race with courage or kindness. Choose one. Picture their face, or what you know of it. What would they say to you, in your last hard mile? The bell holds the time.
Catholic, through the saints: the communion of saints, a great cloud of witnesses who, Catholics believe, still pray with the living. Today's word.
Your line: a cloud of witnesses. Today, when it gets hard, remember the person you named, and run your next mile the way they would. Day two hundred sixty-two.

263.title: Catholic: sacred reading
263.hook: read, reflect, pray and rest on one short passage
263.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns set aside time for lectio divina each day, and many Catholic parishes and other Christians use it in groups, often with the Sunday Gospel: reading a passage several times, sharing a word, praying, and resting in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the saints. Your line was a cloud of witnesses. Whose face came to mind in your hard mile? Day two hundred sixty-three.

How do you read now? Honestly. Headlines, captions, the first line of an email, the top of a thread. Eyes move in a quick zigzag, hunting for the point, and then they're gone. It's efficient. It also means a whole day of words can pass through and leave almost nothing behind. Now a medieval monk, with one page in front of him, reading it so slowly he's almost chewing it. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: lectio divina, sacred reading.
screen: `SKIM, ZIGZAG, GONE.` → `A DAY OF WORDS, NOTHING LEFT.` → `A MONK, CHEWING ONE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Lectio divina is Latin: divine reading, or sacred reading. It's old. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks, sets aside hours every day for holy reading. Much later, a Carthusian monk named Guigo wrote a short letter describing the practice as a ladder with four rungs. The first rung is lectio, reading: slowly, often aloud, a short passage, not a chapter. The second is meditatio, reflecting: you turn one word or phrase over and over, chewing on it. Guigo uses that very picture: reading puts the food in your mouth, meditation chews it. The third is oratio, prayer: you respond, speaking to God from what you heard. The fourth is contemplatio, contemplation: you stop working and simply rest in God's presence, beyond words. He also puts it this way: seek in reading and you'll find in meditation; knock in prayer and contemplation opens the door. Here's a line to try it on. Psalm 45 in the Douay-Rheims numbering, 46 in most others: "Be still and see that I am God." Read it once. Then again, and notice which word catches: still, or see, or God. Stay with that word. Answer it, if you pray. Then stop, and be still. In 2010 Pope Benedict the Sixteenth encouraged the practice for all Catholics, not just monks, and Christians of other churches use it too. The point is not to cover ground. It's to let one short passage cover you.
screen: `LECTIO — READ IT SLOWLY.` · `MEDITATIO — CHEW ON ONE WORD.` · `ORATIO — ANSWER.` · `CONTEMPLATIO — REST.` · then, large: `READ SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one verse four times. Use today's line: be still and see that I am God. First time, just hear it. Second time, notice the one word that catches. Third time, answer it, in prayer if you pray, or in a thought if you don't. Fourth time, let the words go, and simply rest. The bell holds the time.
Lectio divina. Sacred reading: read, reflect, pray, rest, four rungs of a ladder on one short passage. Today's word.
Your line: read slowly. Today, pick one short thing you'd normally skim, a poem, a message, a verse, and read it twice as slowly as usual. Day two hundred sixty-three.

264.title: Catholic: the Hail Mary
264.hook: a prayer drawn from the angel's and Elizabeth's words to Mary (Luke 1:28, 1:42)
264.howItsDone: Catholics learn the Hail Mary as children and pray it on its own, in the rosary, and in the Angelus; its first half comes from Luke's Gospel and its second half asks Mary to pray for us.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lectio divina, one verse read four times. Your line was read slowly. What did you read twice as slowly? Day two hundred sixty-four.

Two women, one old and one very young, both unexpectedly pregnant. The younger one has just traveled into the hill country to see her older cousin. She walks through the door, says hello, and before she can explain anything, the older woman cries out a blessing, and the baby in her own womb leaps. The younger one is Mary. The older one is Elizabeth. Part of what Elizabeth cried out that day is still prayed by Catholics, over and over, in one short prayer. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the Hail Mary.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, BOTH EXPECTING.` → `THE BABY LEAPS.` → `STILL PRAYED TODAY.`

segments.voice: The Hail Mary is built like a mosaic, from pieces of Luke's Gospel. The first piece comes from the angel Gabriel, who visits Mary in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims translation, the Catholic English Bible: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." The second piece comes from Elizabeth, a few verses later: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Put them together, add the name Jesus, and you have the first half of the prayer: all of it straight from scripture. The second half is a request, added later in the Church's history: Mary, the mother of God, is asked to pray for us, now and at the hour of our death. Now look at today's line, full of grace. It comes from a single Greek word Gabriel uses, kecharitomene. You can hear charis inside it, grace, from our week with Christianity. It means something like one who has been graced, favored, filled with favor. The King James Version translates it "highly favoured"; Catholic translations, following Latin, say full of grace. Catholic teaching honors Mary as the mother of Jesus and asks her prayers, as it asks the saints'; Catholics are clear that they don't worship her. Orthodox Christians have a similar prayer that begins with the angel's greeting too. In Protestant churches Mary is honored as a model of faith, and Luke's words are read rather than prayed. For Catholics it's a prayer learned in childhood and repeated ten times in each decade of the rosary.
screen: `THE ANGEL: HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `ELIZABETH: BLESSED ART THOU.` · `THEN A REQUEST: PRAY FOR US.` · `KECHARITOMENE — FILLED WITH FAVOR.` · then, large: `FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it once, slowly. If you pray, you can pray it. If not, just listen to the old greeting as words: hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Then think of someone who has been full of grace toward you, someone who gave more kindness than you earned. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Catholic, through the Hail Mary: a prayer built from the angel's and Elizabeth's greetings to Mary, then a request for her prayers. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace. Today, greet one person the way Elizabeth greeted Mary: with delight that they walked through the door. Day two hundred sixty-four.

265.title: Catholic: works of mercy
265.hook: feed the hungry, visit the sick, welcome the stranger (Matthew 25:35–36)
265.howItsDone: Catholic parishes run food pantries, hospital and prison visits and funeral ministries as works of mercy, and many Catholics choose one work of mercy as a practice, especially during Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hail Mary, the angel's greeting. Your line was full of grace. Did you greet someone with delight? Day two hundred sixty-five.

In one of Jesus' stories, every nation stands before a king on his throne. People are sorted to his right and his left, and they're about to learn what the whole trial was about. The questions ought to be enormous. What did you believe? What did you achieve? Instead the king talks about a plate of food, a visit to someone sick, a spare coat. And everyone, on both sides, is surprised. Today, on our visit to the Catholic tradition: the story behind the works of mercy.
screen: `EVERY NATION BEFORE A KING.` → `WHAT WAS THE TRIAL ABOUT?` → `FOOD, A VISIT, A COAT.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter twenty-five. Jesus tells of the Son of Man coming in glory to judge the nations, and the king says to those on his right, in the Douay-Rheims translation: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in." Naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; in prison, and you came to me. They're confused. When did we ever see you hungry? And the king answers: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." That's the surprise. Nobody on either side knew they'd met him. He was the hungry person. The stranger. The one in the cell. Out of this passage the Catholic Church drew a list: the seven corporal works of mercy, corporal meaning of the body. Feed the hungry. Give drink to the thirsty. Clothe the naked. Shelter the homeless. Visit the sick. Visit the imprisoned. Bury the dead, that last one taken from the book of Tobit. Alongside them sit seven spiritual works of mercy, for the heart and mind: among them, comfort the sorrowful, forgive offenses, bear wrongs patiently, and pray for the living and the dead. Catholic teaching presents these not as extras for especially holy people, but as the everyday shape of faith: a meal, a visit, a coat, a word of comfort.
screen: `THE KING JUDGES THE NATIONS.` · `WHEN DID WE SEE YOU HUNGRY?` · `SEVEN WORKS FOR THE BODY.` · `SEVEN WORKS FOR THE HEART.` · then, large: `I WAS HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one work of mercy for today. Sit, and go through the list slowly in your mind. Hungry. Thirsty. Without clothes, without a home. Sick. In prison. Grieving. Who near you fits one of them? A coworker who skips lunch. A friend in hospital. A neighbor who's lonely. Choose one person and one work. Picture yourself doing it. The bell holds the time.
Catholic, through the works of mercy: seven for the body, seven for the heart, from the king who says I was hungry. Today's word.
Your line: I was hungry. Today, do the one work of mercy you chose, however small, and look closely at the face in front of you. Day two hundred sixty-five.

266.title: Lent, forty days
266.hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter
266.howItsDone: Catholics begin Lent with ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast that day and on Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays, and take on personal practices of prayer, fasting and almsgiving until Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the works of mercy, and the king who said I was hungry. Which work did you choose? Day two hundred sixty-six, the last day of our visit to the Catholic tradition.

One Wednesday in late winter, you might notice something odd on the train. A smudge of gray on someone's forehead. Then another, and another: a nurse, a guy in a suit, a teenager with earbuds. It isn't dirt. It's ash, put there that morning in the shape of a cross, with a few old words: remember that you are dust. It's the first day of a season that runs forty days, and it asks people to give something up. Today, to end our week with the Catholic tradition: Lent.
screen: `A GRAY SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `REMEMBER THAT YOU ARE DUST.` → `FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: The ashes come from Genesis, from God's words to Adam, in the Douay-Rheims translation: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim, but some hear it as freeing: you're not in charge of everything, and the time you have is a gift. Why forty? Because forty keeps turning up in the Bible as a time of testing and preparation: forty days of rain for Noah, forty years for Israel in the wilderness, forty days for Moses on the mountain. And Jesus fasted forty days in the desert before he began to teach. Lent follows him there. It's a season of three practices, all from Jesus' teaching in Matthew six: prayer, fasting and almsgiving, which means giving to the poor. Catholic practice asks for fasting on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and no meat on the Fridays of Lent. People often choose a personal sacrifice too, sweets, social media, a daily coffee, or add something good instead. If you count the days from Ash Wednesday to Easter, you get more than forty; in the Western count, Sundays aren't counted, since each Sunday is kept as a small Easter. Orthodox Christians keep their own Great Lent, starting on a Monday. The English name Lent comes from an old word for spring, the season of lengthening days. Now look back at our week. The Eucharist: real presence. The rosary: one bead at a time. The saints: a cloud of witnesses. Sacred reading: read slowly. The Hail Mary: full of grace. The works of mercy: I was hungry. And Lent: forty days, walking toward Easter.
screen: `FOR DUST THOU ART.` · `FORTY: TESTING AND PREPARING.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LENT — THE LENGTHENING DAYS.` · then, large: `FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give up one small thing for a day. Sit, and look honestly at your day. What do you reach for without thinking? The phone at red lights. A second dessert. A sharp comment. Choose one, just for today. Picture the moment you'll want it, and what you'll do with that gap instead: a breath, a prayer if you pray, a coin for someone. The bell holds the time.
Lent. From the old English word for spring: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving on the way to Easter. Today's word.
Your line: forty days. Today, keep your one small fast, and when the gap opens, fill it with something good. Day two hundred sixty-six. Tomorrow we visit Islam.

options: good luck this season.
remember that you are dust.
you are forgiven.
fork.reveal: one traditional formula echoes Genesis 3:19: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

trapdoor: what you thought: giving up chocolate.
what it means: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, following Jesus into the desert, on the way to Easter.
what a scholar hears: Latin calls it Quadragesima, 'the fortieth'; English 'Lent' is from lencten, spring; Sundays are left out of the Western count.
